newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: No obvious successor to Zimbabwe's ageing Mugabe.
newsitem.headline: No obvious successor to Zimbabwe's ageing Mugabe.

text.p: Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe turns 73 on Friday. Secure in power, he plans to mark the day with pomp reserved elsewhere for royalty.
But his southern African nation is privately unsettled by the absence of an obvious successor to the man who has ruled it with little challenge over the last 17 years.

Mugabe is believed to be preparing to retire at end of his current six-year term in 2002, but efforts by some politicians to open up a public debate on the issue have been muffled by top leaders over the years.
The Zimbabwean leader has personally discouraged open discussion of the succession, saying his dominant ruling ZANU-PF party will settle the question "whenever" the time came for him to go.
For the birthday celebrations in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe's second city, ZANU-PF has organised theatre groups, choirs and traditional dancers to perform at banquets for 3,000 guests.

The state presidency has no fixed term, and some Zimbabweans speculate that newly remarried Mugabe may be persuaded by his 32-year-old wife, former presidential secretary Grace Marufu, to seek another term in 2002.

While the country mulls that prospect, independent media and some outspoken political commentators keep floating the issue of a smooth succession, saying economic growth, investment and social stability require some high level of political predictability.

"We must encourage debate over every issue. We must try to build fairly predictable systems, based on democracy, as they are doing in most of Western Europe and North America," says John Makumbe, a political analyst at Harare's University of Zimbabwe.
"Unless there are efforts to impose some leaders behind our backs, it's only fair that those seeking high office come forward and have their merits and demerits debated," he added.
"We should take a leaf from South Africa where Mandela has a clearer exit programme and the succession issue is not regarded as sacrosanct," he said.
President Nelson Mandela has told South Africans he plans to step down in 1999 at the end of his term, and has indicated that he would back Deputy President Thabo Mbeki as his successor.

Zimbabweans can safely assume that whoever he or she is, the next president will emerge from ZANU-PF. The party currently controls 147 of the 150 seats in parliament, and the opposition is too weak and fragmented to offer an alternative.
Although the succession debate was squeezed out of ZANU-PF's agenda at a national conference last December, the issue remains alive in private, and so too is the race to succeed Mugabe.

Mugabe's two vice-presidents, both of them members of the ruling party and the government, are ruled out of contest on account of their age: veteran nationalist Joshua Nkomo is 80, and Simon Muzenda is 75.
But Makumbe, and Charles Rukuni, publisher and editor of an independent Zimbabwean political and economic newsletter, The Insider, say the race is still very crowded.

"It can be one of a dozen or so contenders. I don't think anybody has anything clearly sewn up yet," said Makumbe, whose list of possible successors include former army commanders, Solomon Mujuru and Josiah Tungamirai, State Security Minister Sydney Sekeramayi and Justice Minister Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Others regularly mentioned in connection with Mugabe's job are Commerce and Industry Minister Nathan Shamuyarira, Minister Without Portfolio Eddison Zvobgo, Lands and Water Resources Minister Kumbirai Kangai, Home (Interior) Affairs Minister Dumiso Dabengwa and Local Government Minister John Nkomo.
Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa, Higher Education Minister Ignatious Chombo and Foreign Affairs Minister Stan Mudenge are also mentioned as potential contenders.
None has the national profile of Mugabe and all would have to build solid regional alliances to seriously gun for the top job, political analysts say.
"In terms of policy, I don't see any serious changes: I think many of them admire Mugabe's mixture of hard rhetoric and some kind of pragmatics on the ground," Rukuni says.
But the pressure-cooker atmosphere created by the chief's apparent reluctance to contemplate his passing from the scene is having its effects on the ruling group.
Factional fights in ZANU-PF have increased as leaders jostle for positions, and some political analysts say the party may suffer damaging splits along regional/ethnic lines as a result.
